parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -able, from Old French -able, from Latin -ābilis.

parole.significato: suffix used to form noun (uppercase) demonyms
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ain, from Old French -ain, from Latin -ānus, whence also French -an and -ien.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin -ārium, the accusative of -ārius; or (in the feminine) from -āria. Compare the inherited doublet of -ier/-ière.

parole.significato: -al; appended to various words, often nouns, to make an adjective form; often added to words of Latin origin, but used…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -al, from Old French -al, borrowed from Latin -ālis. Doublet of -el, which is inherited. The masculine plural in -x comes from the letter's usage as a ligature to abbreviate -us.
Derived from Latin -ātus, -ātūs (whence also English -ate, -y). Doublet of -é (abstract noun suffix), which is inherited. See also the etymology at English -ate.

parole.significato: found in borrowed Latin past participles (sometimes nominalized)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -ātus, -ātī (whence also English -ate, -ee). Doublet of -é (past participle suffix), which is inherited. See also the etymology at English -ate.

Learned borrowing from Latin -ātus (perfect passive participle suffix). These chemistry nouns originated as substantivized perfect passive participles from first conjugation Latin verbs; e.g. the Latin adjective acētātus in the 18th-century Latin phrase plumbum acētātum (“lead acetate”, literally “a
Learned borrowing from Latin -ātōrem. Doublet of -eur.

parole.significato: Used to indicate action, condition, result or effect; -ation
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ation, from Old French -ation, a learned borrowing from Latin -ātiō, from -tiō, from Proto-Italic *-tiō, from Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō, from *-tis + *-Hō. In words inherited through Vulgar Latin, the same suffix yielded -aison.

parole.significato: forms the feminine of nouns referring to people
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French -e, from Latin -am, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂.
Inherited from Old French -el, from Latin -ālis. Doublet of -al.
Borrowed from Latin -entia. Compare Italian -enza, Portuguese -ença, -ência, Romanian -ință, -ență, Spanish -enza, -encia. Doublet of -ance, which is inherited.

parole.significato: used to form nouns describing the condition of being something (-ness, -ity, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French -ece, from Latin -itia. The modern spelling is due to a phonetic merger with etymology 2; see below. Related to -ise.

parole.significato: forms masculine agent nouns from verbs (some of which are also used as adjectives)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -eur, from Old French -or / -eor / -eur, from Latin -tōrem and -ātōrem, from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr. Doublet of -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French -eur, from Old French -or, from Latin -ōrem, from Proto-Italic *-ōs, from Proto-Indo-European *-ōs.
Inherited from Middle French -eux, -eulx, from Old French -eux, -eus, -us, -os, -ous, from Latin -ōsus. Doublet of -ose.
Borrowed from Latin -fer.
Inherited from Old French -ible, from Latin -ibilis.
Borrowed from Latin -idus.

parole.significato: indicates a feminine noun, often an abstract one
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ie, from Old French -ie, from Latin -ia.
Inherited from Latin -īnus, from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos.
Inherited from Middle French -ique, from Old French -ique, a learned borrowing from Latin -icus, from Proto-Italic *-ikos, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikos.

parole.significato: Attaches to an adjective in the feminine singular to form the corresponding adverb.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ment, from Old French -ment, from Latin mente.

parole.significato: forms nouns from verbs, usually indicating a resulting action or state
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ment, from Old French -ment, from Latin -mentum.

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of some verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of second conjugation verbs. Compare Italian -ere, Romanian -ea, Romansh -air.
Borrowed from Latin -ōsus; doublet of the inherited -eux.

parole.significato: forms adjectives having the sense of ‘having quality of, being provided with’ (the root word)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ūtus.

Inherited from Middle French -é, from Old French -é, from Latin -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns) (fourth declension), from Proto-Italic *-tus, from Proto-Indo-European *-tus (suffix deriving action nouns from verb roots). Doublet of -at (abstract noun).

parole.significato: forms a feminine noun indicating a quantity or content measured by what the base noun denotes, often translatable as -f…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ee f, from Old French -ee, from Latin -ātam (accusative of -āta), whence also -ade, which is borrowed from other Romance languages.

parole.significato: A prefix forming words, especially verbs, that denote entering a state, making progress toward a goal, or the like.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French a-, from Latin ad-.
Learned borrowing from Latin acerbus.

parole.significato: wing (of a bird or other flying animal; of poultry; of an aircraft; of a building; of an army; in football and rugby; i…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French aisle, from Old French aile, from Latin āla (“wing [of animals]”).
From Latin album.
Borrowed from Latin alter (“other”).
From Old French, from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).
Borrowed from Latin apertus (“open”). Doublet of ouvert.
Borrowed from Latin apicem (“point, tip”).
Borrowed from Latin aptus.
Borrowed from Latin aqua.
Learned borrowing from Latin arguere.
Borrowed from Latin aurōra.

parole.significato: to have; to own; to possess; to get
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French avoir, from Old French avoir, aveir, aver, from Latin habēre (“have, hold, possess”), probably from a Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰh₁bʰ- (“to grab, to take”). Influenced and reinforced by similar (yet etymologically unrel
Inherited from Middle French barbe, from Old French barbe, from Latin barba, from earlier *farba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”).
From Latin bis (“twice”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bis (“twice”).

Inherited from Middle French boire, from Old French boivre, beivre, from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Inherited from Middle French bon, from Old French bon, from Latin bonus (“good”), from Old Latin duenos, later duonus, from Proto-Italic *dwenos.
Inherited from Old French brume, borrowed from Latin brūma (“winter”), possibly through the intermediate of Old Occitan bruma.

Inherited from Middle French bœuf, from Old French buef, boef, from Latin bovem (“ox”), from Proto-Italic *gʷōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (compare English cow). The music sense derives from the expression “faire un Bœuf”, after the Parisian cabaret-bar Le Bœuf sur le toit where jam

parole.significato: Cancer (someone born with a Cancer star sign)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cancer.
Borrowed from Latin cancer. Doublet of chancre and cancer.
Borrowed from Latin caprīnus. Compare chèvre.
Borrowed from Latin capsa. Doublet of casse, caisse, and châsse.
Inherited from Old French cause, borrowed from Classical Latin causa. Compare chose, an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Middle French cent, from Old French cent, from Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.
Borrowed from Latin centi-, from centum (“hundred”).

Inherited from Middle French cerveau, cervel, from Old French cervel, from Latin cerebellum, diminutive of cerebrum, from Proto-Italic *kerazrom, from a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱerh₂-s-ro, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”).
Inherited from Middle French chair, char, from Old French char, charn (earlier carn), from Latin carnem, carō, from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *(s)ker-. Doublet of carne.

parole.significato: to matter (to), to be of import (for)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French chaloir, from Old French chaloir, from earlier chaleir, from Latin calēre (“to heat”), from Proto-Italic *kalēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-. Compare Occitan caler, Catalan caldre (“to be necessary”), Italian calere.

Inherited from Middle French chancre, from Old French chancre, inherited from Latin cancrum, from Proto-Italic *kankros, dissimilation of *karkros (“enclosure”) (because the pincers of a crab form a circle), from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
Inherited from Latin calvus.
Inherited from Middle French cher, from Old French cher, chier, from Latin cārum (“dear, valuable”), from Proto-Italic *kāros, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros, from *keh₂- (“to desire, to wish”).
Inherited from Middle French ciel, from Old French ciel, from Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.
Borrowed from Latin cippus (“stake”). Doublet of cep.
Learned borrowing from Latin classis.
Inherited from Old French clou, from Latin clāvus, from Proto-Italic *klāwos, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u-.

Inherited from Middle French clef, from Old French clef, from Latin clāvis, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kleh₂w-. According to Bescherelle, the spelling clé had replaced clef by 1845.
Learned borrowing from Latin colōnus.
Inherited from Old French comun, from Latin commūnis.
Inherited from Middle French cors, from Old French cors, inherited from Latin corpus (“body”). The p was added back to reflect the Latin etymology. Doublet of corpus.

parole.significato: a corpus, a body of texts
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin corpus (“body”). Doublet of corps.
Inherited from Middle French couleur, from Old French color, from Latin colōrem m.

parole.significato: a category of severe offences within French law, comparable to a felony under United States laws. Crime are tied to the…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French crimne, borrowed from Latin crīmen, from Proto-Italic *kreimen, from Proto-Indo-European *kréymn̥, from *krey- (“sieve”) + *-mn̥.
Inherited from Latin corium.
From Middle French and Old French cene, an ecclesiastical borrowing from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kert(e)snā, from Proto-Indo-European *kert-sna, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *sker-.
Borrowed from Latin cēdere.
Inherited from Middle French de, from Old French de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁.
Inherited from Middle French deux, from Old French deus, from Latin duōs, masculine accusative plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.
Inherited from Middle French dieu, from Old French deu, from Latin deus, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós.

parole.significato: to say, to tell (to express through speech)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French dire, from Old French dire, from Latin dīcō, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).
Borrowed from Latin dis-. Compare the inherited dé-.
Inherited from Middle French dormir, from Old French dormir, from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin dūrus.
Inherited from Middle French des-, from Old French des-, from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís.

parole.significato: water, a liquid that is transparent, colorless, odorless, and tasteless in its pure form, the primary constituent of la…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French eau, eaue, from Old French ewe, euwe, egua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water, flowing water”), related to Frankish *ahu ~ ahwā (“stream, water”). See also English ea (“watercourse, river”). Cognates See also Angevin ave, eiv

parole.significato: in (used to indicate space, also see usage notes)
parole.testo: From Middle French en, from Old French en, from Latin in, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).
Inherited from Old French en-, from Latin in-, prefixation of Latin in (“in, into”); see en.
Learned borrowing from Latin facultās. Doublet of facilité.

From Middle French faire, from Old French faire, from Latin facere. The past historic and imperfect subjunctive stem fi- (fis, fis, fit...) originated in the Latin form fēcī, with metaphony (*/ˈfed͡zi/ > */ˈfit͡s/).

parole.significato: to stuff; to put stuffing in something
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin farcīre (“to cram, to stuff”).
Inherited from Middle French faulx, from Old French fauz, faus, fals, from Latin falsus.

parole.significato: to split, to chop (wood), to crack
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French fendre, from Latin findere, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).

Inherited from Middle French ferme, from Old French ferm, ferme (“solid”), from Latin firmus (“solid, secure”), from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).
Inherited from Middle French fixe.

parole.significato: flower; bloom; blossom; collectively, the reproductive organs and the envelope which surrounds them in angiosperms (als…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French flur, flour, flor, from Latin flōrem (“flower; the finest part of something”), from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-s (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰleh₃- (“to bloom”). In some senses, from Middle French fleur (“surface, upper side, top layer”), ultimatel
Inherited from Old French fondre, from Latin fundere (“to melt”), from Proto-Italic *hundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-.
Inherited from Old French funz (“cultivated or developed land”), from Latin fundus. Doublet of fond.
Inherited from Latin forum; doublet of fur and forum. Unrelated to French fort.
Learned borrowing from Latin forceps.
Inherited from Old French fort, from Latin fortem (“strong”), from Old Latin forctis, fortis.
Inherited from Middle French four, from Old French four, forz, forn, from Latin furnus, from Proto-Italic *fornos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰr̥-nós, from *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).

parole.significato: brother (son of the same parents as another person)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French frere, from older fredre, fradre, from Latin frātrem, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

parole.significato: only used in au fur et à mesure (“gradually, as you go along”)

Inherited from Middle French, Old French ferir, from Latin ferīre.
Borrowed from Latin germen.
Borrowed from Latin glūten (“glue”).
Inherited from Middle French goust, from Old French goust, from Latin gustus, from Proto-Italic *gustus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.
Borrowed from Latin gerere.

Inherited from Middle French homme, from Old French home, hom, hume, homme, etc, from Latin hominem (with the loss of the -in- syllable, via syncope and then assimilation of -mn- to -mm-), from Old Latin hemō, from Proto-Italic *hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ (“earthling”). Compare Catalan hom

Inherited from Middle French hoste, from Old French oste, from Latin hospitem, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European root *gʰóstipotis, a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. See also Old French ost.
Borrowed from Latin in-, from Proto-Italic *n̥-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, from *né.
Learned borrowing from Latin inter. Doublet of entre-.
Learned borrowing from Latin integer. Doublet of entier.
Inherited from Old French joindre, from Latin iungere (“join”), from Proto-Italic *jungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yunégti ~ *yungénti, from the root *yewg-.
Inherited from Middle French joug, from Old French jug, jou, jof, from Latin jugum, iugum, from Proto-Italic *jugom, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.

parole.significato: to be jubilant or ecstatic, to exult
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūbilāre.
From Middle French la, from Old French la, from Latin illam, which is the accusative singular feminine of ille.
Inherited from Middle French lac, from Old French lac, which displaced earlier lai (“pit, trench, ditch, grave, mere, pond”, see in lac). Generally inferred as a borrowing of Latin lacus (“lake”).
From Middle French le, from Old French le, from Latin illum, by dropping il- and -m. Latin illum is the accusative singular of ille.

Inherited from Middle French libre, from Old French libre, semi-learned form of livre (ca. 1200), from Latin līber (“free”), from Old Latin loeber, from Proto-Italic *louðeros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-er-os, from *h₁lewdʰ- (“people”).
Inherited from Middle French lieu, from Old French leu, from Latin locum, from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”).
Inherited from Old French lire, from Latin legere, from Proto-Italic *legō, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-.
Inherited from Middle French livre, from Old French livre, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin librum. The strictly inherited form would be *loivre. Doublet of liber.
Inherited from Middle French loy, from Old French loi, lei, from Latin lēgem, from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s < *leǵ-.
Learned borrowing from Latin lucrum.
Borrowed from Latin lumen.
Inherited from Middle French lune, from Old French lune, from Latin lūna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, from *lewk- + *-sneh₂.

Inherited from Middle French main, Old French main, mein, man, from Latin manus (“hand”), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entr
Inherited from Old French maire m, from Latin maior m (“forefathers; mayor”). Compare the doublet majeur.
From Middle French majeur, a borrowing from Latin maior (“larger, greater”). Doublet of maire, major, and mayeur.
Inherited from Middle French mal-, from Old French mal-, from mal (“bad; badly”).
Inherited from Middle French maistre, from Old French maistre, from Latin magistrum. Doublet of maestro, borrowed from Italian, magister, borrowed from Latin, and master, borrowed from English.

Inherited from Middle French mer, from Old French mer, from Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. The word is almost unparalleled as a Latin neuter that has become feminine without being a backformation from a plural in -a (French -e). This has been ascribed to the inf
Inherited from Middle French mille, from Old French mile, from Latin mīlle (“thousand”) (plural mīlia), from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”).
From Latin mille (“thousand”).
From Old French, borrowed from Latin minister.

parole.significato: minute (etymology 1, time unit, all same senses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French minute, borrowed from Latin minūta. Compare menu, an inherited doublet.

Inherited from Middle French mode, from Old French mode f, ultimately from Latin modus m. The masculine gender was reintroduced for some senses during the Middle French period under influence of the Latin. Doublet of mœuf.
Inherited from Middle French mort, from Old French mort, from Latin mors.
Inherited from Middle French mourir, from Old French morir, from Latin morīrī, variant of morī.
Learned borrowing from Latin mūcus.
Inherited from Middle French mur, from Old French mur, from Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Italic *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).
Inherited from Middle French mere, from Old French medre, mere, from Latin mātrem, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
Borrowed from Latin meritum.
Inherited from Middle French nation, from Old French nacion, borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French neveu, from Latin nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts.
Inherited from Old French nid, from Latin nīdus, from Proto-Italic *nizdos (“nest”), from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”).

Inherited from Old French nom (whence Norman nom), from Latin nōmen (whence Italian and Portuguese nome; Spanish nombre), from Proto-Italic *nomən, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (whence Ancient Greek ὄνομα (ónoma), Russian и́мя (ímja), Sanskrit नामन् (nā́man), English name).
Borrowed from Latin nota.

parole.significato: the plural personal pronoun in the first person:
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French nous, from Old French nous, nos, from Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs. In several dialects of French, je may be used instead of nous (j'allons instead of nous allons, je voyons instead of nous voyons etc.), this use was perceived as peasant-like and thus often mocked s
Inherited from Old French novembre, from Latin novembrem.
Borrowed from Latin novāre.
Inherited from Middle French nuyt, from Old French noit, from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Inherited from Old French octobre, borrowed from Latin Octōbrem. Replaced the inherited Old French uitovre. Compare also the Old French form witembre from the Vulgar Latin variant octember.
Ellipsis of voiture omnibus (“carriage for all”), the latter element being a learned borrowing from Latin omnibus (“for all”), dative plural of omnis (“all”).
Borrowed from Latin opus. Doublet of œuvre and opéra.
From Middle French or, from Old French or, from Latin aurum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- (“glow”), from *h₂ews- (“to dawn, become light, become red”).

Inherited from Old French oaille, from earlier oeille (with the ending subsequently matched to the suffix -aille), from Latin ovicula, diminutive of ovis, from Proto-Italic *owis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis.

Inherited from Middle French ours, from Old French urs, from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos. The Early Modern French pronunciation was /uʁ/ before consonants, /uʁz/ before vowels, and /uʁs/ in pausa. For the most part, the pausal pronunciations were eventua

parole.significato: per-; throughly; extremely; to an end
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin per-.
From Old French part, from Latin partem, accusative of pars, from Proto-Italic *partis.
Borrowed from Latin patera.
Inherited from Old French paistre, from Latin pāscere, from Proto-Italic *pāskō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect”).
Inherited from Old French penne f, from Latin pinna f, penna f, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”). Doublet of panne. See also pinacle–panache.

parole.significato: to weigh (to have a weight of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French peser, from Old French peser, from Classical Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet penser 'think'.

Inherited from Old French poi, from Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare Catalan poc, Italian poco, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco. Cognate with English few.

Inherited from Middle French peuple, from Old French pueple, semi-learned form of pueble, from earliest Old French poblo (9th c.), from Latin populus, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”). Doublet of people and pueblo.
Inherited from Middle French pieux, from Old French piu(s) (later changed on the basis of adjectives ending in -eux), from Latin pius.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Probably; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: Middle French pilori, from Old French pilori, of uncertain origin, probably via Old Occitan espilori and/or Old Catalan from Latin pīla.

Inherited from Old French piz, peiz (“chest, udder”), inherited from Latin pectus, from Proto-Italic *pektos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peg- (“breast”). The word underwent a semantic shift beginning in Old French and was gradually replaced by poitrine in the sense of “chest”.
Borrowed from Latin plānus. Doublet of plain, which was inherited, and piano.
Inherited from Old French, inherited from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”), from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from *pleh₂- (“flat”).

Inherited from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple; Italian pieno; Portuguese cheio; Romanian plin; Sardinian prenu; Spanish lleno; English plene, full.
Inherited from Old French plume, from Latin plūma.
Inherited from Middle French poing (“fist”), from Old French poing (“hand”), from Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, *puḱnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
Inherited from Middle French poinct (with orthography modified to reflect the Latin etymology), from Old French point, from Latin pūnctum.

Inherited from Middle French pomme, from Old French pome, from Latin pōma, plural of pōmum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular, from Proto-Italic *poomos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”). Compare English pome.
Inherited from Old French pondre, inherited from Latin pōnere, from Proto-Italic *pozinō. False friend to Spanish poner, although being cognates.
Inherited from Middle French porc, from Old French porc, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”).
Inherited from Old French port, borrowed from Latin portus, from Proto-Italic *portus, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”), from *per- (“to go forth, to cross”).
Learned borrowing from Latin posterior.
Inherited from Old French pris, from Latin pretium (“price, reward”), from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”). Compare précieux.
Inherited from Middle French pere, from Old French pedre, pedra, pere, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.
Borrowed from Latin quadri- (“four”).
Inherited from Latin quem.
Learned borrowing from Latin quid. Doublet of que and quoi.
From one combining form of Latin quīnque (“five”) (see, for example, quindecim, whence French quinze), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe (“five; hand”).
Borrowed from Latin quōrum.
From Middle French ragoûter (“to awaken the appetite”), from goût (“taste”), from Latin gustus.
Inherited from Middle French roy, from Old French roi, rei, from Latin rēgem.
Learned borrowing from Latin retrō. Compare arrière.
Borrowed from Latin sacrāre.

parole.significato: a male saint; masculine of sainte
parole.testo: From Latin sanctus (“holy”).
Borrowed from Latin salūbrem.
Borrowed from Latin scindere.

Inherited from Old French sein, from Latin sinus, from Proto-Italic *sinus, from Proto-Indo-European *sinos. Doublet of sinus. Compare Italian seno, Romanian sân, Romansh sain, Portuguese seio, Spanish seno.
Inherited from Middle French selle, from Old French sele, from Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.

parole.significato: to be suitable for; to be proper for
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French seoir, from Old French seoir, from earlier sedeir, from Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.

parole.significato: September (the ninth month of the Gregorian calendar, following August and preceding October, containing the southward…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Septembrem. Compare Old French setembre, sietembre.
Inherited from Middle French serpent, from Old French serpent, from Latin serpentem, accusative form of serpēns.

parole.significato: to serve (to help in a shop; to bring a meal to someone)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French servir, from Old French servir, from Latin servīre.
Borrowed from Latin saeta.

Inherited from Middle French soye, from Old French soie, earlier seie, from Latin sēta, saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”).
Borrowed from Latin solidus. Doublet of sou.

parole.significato: fate, destiny (consequences or effects predetermined by past events or a divine will)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French sort, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Cf. also the borrowed doublet sorte.
From Latin sub, via Old French sus-, sous- (the spelling with s by analogy with the preposition sous < Latin subtus).
Learned borrowing from Latin stipula. Doublet of éteule.
Learned borrowing from Latin super-. Doublet of sur-.

Inherited from Middle French sur, from Old French sur, seur, sor, soure, souvre, sovre (“on, upon, over”), from Latin super (“over, on, above”). Doublet of super, a borrowing. Cognate with Old English ofer (“over, above”). More at over.
Inherited from Old French sur-, sour-, from syncopation of Latin super-. Doublet of super-.
Borrowed from Latin serum.

parole.significato: sister (a daughter of the same parents as another person; a female sibling)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French soeur, from Old French suer (nominative), from Latin soror (cf. also the Old French oblique form seror from the Latin accusative sorōrem), from Proto-Italic *swezōr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
Learned borrowing from Latin tacitus.
Learned borrowing from Latin tangēns.

parole.significato: b; designating a third house with the same number
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ter.
Inherited from Old French terme, inherited from Latin terminus, from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”). Doublet of terminus.
Inherited from Old French tiers, from Latin tertius.
Learned borrowing from Latin trāns. Doublet of très.
Learned borrowing from Latin trāns. Doublet of très and trans.
Inherited from Old French trois, treis, from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
From Old French tu, from Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognates with the exact same usage are the Italian tu, as well as du in German or ты in Russian.
Borrowed from Latin tenebrae.
Learned borrowing from Latin ulcus, ulceris.
Borrowed from Latin ultimus.
Inherited from Middle French un, from Old French un, from Latin ūnum, accusative singular of ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.

Inherited from Old French veintre, later veincre, vencre, inherited from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, nasal infix from *weyk- (“to overcome”). The current pronunciation is influenced by the first-person singular indicative present form vincō. Compare al
Inherited from Middle French valoir, from Old French valoir, valeir, from Latin valēre, from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥h₁éh₁yeti, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule, be strong”).
Inherited from Middle French vase, borrowed from Latin vās.

parole.significato: to come (to move from one place to another that is nearer the speaker)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French venir, from Old French venir, from Latin venīre.
Inherited from Middle French vent, from Old French vent, from Latin ventus, from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts < *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
Inherited from Old French ver, verm (“worm”), from Latin vermem (“worm”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.

Inherited from Middle French voirre (most probably pronounced /ˈvwɛːrə/), from Old French voirre, from Latin vitrum. Doublet of vitre. The irregular evolution of /wɛ/ into /ɛ/ in this word is "early but normal after labials"; the influence of derivatives with an etymological first-syllable /ɛ/ may a
Inherited from Latin vicia.

parole.significato: life, the state of organisms (organic beings) prior to death
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French vie, from older Old French viḍe, from Vulgar Latin vītam, from the accusative of Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā.
Inherited from Middle French vif, from Old French vif, from Latin vīvus (“alive, living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
Borrowed from Latin vigil.
Inherited from Middle French ville, from Old French ville, vile, inherited from Latin vīlla (“country house”). Doublet of villa.
Inherited from Middle French vin, from Old French vin, from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.
Borrowed from Latin vīrus.
Inherited from Old French vis, from Latin vītis (“vine”).

parole.significato: a mark or stamp attesting to the performance of an official action
parole.testo: From Latin visa, neuter plural of Latin visus (“having been seen”).
Borrowed from Latin vitrum. Doublet of verre. Compare Spanish vidrio and Catalan vidre.

Inherited from Middle French vivre, from Old French vivre, from Latin vīvere. Forms in véc- originate from Latin irregular perfect stem vīx- (vīxī, vīxistī, ...) undergoing metathesis and shortening to vĭsc-.
Inherited from Old French voie, veie, inherited from Latin via. Doublet of via. Unrelated to voir and voirie, despite influencing the latter.

Inherited from Middle French veoir, from Old French veoir, veir, from earlier vedeir, from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Unrelated to voie and its derivatives and to voirie or avoir. See cognates in regional languages in France : Norman veî or ve
Inherited from Middle French voix, from Old French voiz, from Latin vōcem, accusative of vōx (“voice”), from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs.
Learned borrowing from Latin vortex.

parole.significato: the plural personal pronoun in the second person
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French vous, from Old French vos, vous, from Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs. See cognates in regional languages in France: Angevin, Bourbonnais-Berrichon, Bourguignon, Champenois, Lorrain, Orléanais, and Poitevin-Saintongeais vous; Franc-Comtois vôs; Gallo vouz; Norman and F
Inherited from Old French a, a merge of Latin ad and ab.
Inherited from Middle French ame, amme, from Old French ame, anme, anima, from Latin anima. Compare dialectal English onde (“breath”), Gothic 𐌰𐌷𐌼𐌰 (ahma, “spirit”).
Inherited from Middle French espine, from Old French espine, from Latin spīna, from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”).
